blockers.title: Inconsistent data quality management across AI use cases
blockers.statement: The organisation lacks consistent practices, responsibilities and criteria for defining, assessing and maintaining the level of data quality required for different AI use cases and data sources.
blockers.cluster: 6) Data, Architecture, security & Sharing foundations (Organizational side.)
blockers.why_it_matters: AI use cases have different requirements for accuracy, completeness, consistency and reliability. Railway infrastructure managers need agreed quality expectations, standards and responsibilities so that data is fit for its intended operational purpose and can be reused confidently across initiatives.
blockers.consequence: AI initiatives may repeatedly spend effort assessing and correcting data, apply inconsistent quality thresholds, produce unreliable results or fail to scale because the suitability of data cannot be demonstrated consistently.

blockers.title: Weak MVP and incremental delivery discipline
blockers.statement: AI initiatives lack a disciplined pathway from experimentation towards usable products, with insufficient focus on MVPs, intermediate prototypes and incremental validation in realistic operational conditions.
blockers.cluster: 9) Delivery approach, MVP Focus & Timing constraints
blockers.why_it_matters: Scaling requires organisations to learn progressively whether a solution works technically, operationally and for its users. MVPs and intermediate prototypes provide opportunities to test assumptions, gather feedback and increase maturity before committing to full-scale deployment.
blockers.consequence: Projects may remain as repeated PoCs or demonstrations, make large jumps in complexity towards production, and reach later stages without sufficient evidence of operational fit, user acceptance or readiness to scale.

blockers.title: Unclear financial implications, risks and investment logic
blockers.statement: Financial implications, risks and investment logic are not explicitly addressed when preparing AI initiatives for scale, including how shared data, integration, platform and governance foundations should be funded and allocated across multiple use cases.
blockers.why_it_matters: Decision-makers need a clear view of costs, benefits, risks and financial exposure before committing resources, particularly where AI investment competes with long-term infrastructure, maintenance and safety-related expenditure. This also requires recognising that some data, integration, platform and governance capabilities are shared foundations that create value across multiple AI initiatives rather than costs attributable to a single use case.
blockers.consequence: Individual use cases may appear unnecessarily expensive or financially unattractive, shared capabilities may be underfunded or repeatedly rebuilt, and commitment to scale may weaken because stakeholders cannot justify investment or manage financial risk.
blockers.stakeholders: Executive / senior management; Asset management; Legal / safety / compliance; Data science / AI teams; Asset Owner (technical owner of asset) ; ERP  (SAP/Maximo) IT Managers; (SAP/Maximo) Business Application Managers

blockers.why_it_matters: Infrastructure managers need reproducible deployment, logging, telemetry, support and handover so AI solutions can operate reliably beyond the pilot stage.
blockers.consequence: Solutions may remain experimental, fail in live use or become difficult to maintain, monitor and improve over time.
blockers.stakeholders: IT / data platform; Data science / AI teams; Maintenance / operations; Asset management; Systems engineering; Asset Owner (technical owner of asset) ; ERP  (SAP/Maximo) IT Managers; (SAP/Maximo) Business Application Managers

blockers.title: Limited explainability, interpretability and field trust
blockers.statement: AI outputs are not sufficiently explainable or interpretable for the people who need to use and trust them in the field.
blockers.why_it_matters: Field and asset management users need to understand AI outputs well enough to trust, challenge and act on them in safety-conscious infrastructure contexts.
blockers.consequence: Users may reject or bypass AI tools, limiting adoption and preventing progression towards more autonomous AI-supported decisions.

blockers.title: Organisational data silos limiting reuse and scaling
blockers.statement: Organisational data silos limit data reuse, interoperability and scaling across AI initiatives.

blockers.title: Safety implications not identified early
blockers.statement: Safety implications, potential failure modes and the role of human oversight are not identified early enough when framing AI use cases.
blockers.why_it_matters: AI may influence maintenance or operational decisions with safety implications. Identifying these implications early allows assurance, accountability and evidence requirements to be designed into the initiative rather than discovered late.
blockers.consequence: Safety requirements may emerge late, forcing redesign, limiting deployment scope, delaying approval or preventing the solution from progressing to operational use.

blockers.title: Difficulty proving safety and reliability at scale
blockers.statement: AI systems are difficult to prove safe and reliable when moving from pilots to scaled operational use.
blockers.why_it_matters: Safety-critical railway environments need clear assurance, applicable standards and validated evidence before AI can support operational decisions.
blockers.consequence: AI initiatives may be delayed, restricted or rejected because safety, reliability and certification expectations cannot be demonstrated.

source_attributes.Cluster: Operational fit, supplier steering & support package
source_attributes.enabler_description: Use a structured assessment process to compare candidate technologies, algorithms, platforms and delivery approaches before committing to a solution.
source_attributes.practical_actions: Compare alternative technologies and algorithms against operational requirements; assess off-the-shelf versus bespoke solutions; evaluate scalability, integration, supportability and vendor dependency; assess platform compatibility; test promising options with users before committing to more advanced development.
source_attributes.expected_outcome: AI initiatives select solutions that better fit operational needs and have a clearer pathway to integration, support and scaling, reducing the risk of technical dead ends or costly redesign.
source_attributes.stakeholders: Asset management; Maintenance / operations; Systems engineering; IT / data platform; Data science / AI team

enablers.enabler_description: Assess safety implications at the earliest stages of an AI initiative to determine whether the use case may influence safety-relevant decisions and what level of assurance and human oversight may be required.
enablers.practical_actions: Identify safety-relevant outputs and decisions; consider credible failure modes and consequences; define human oversight and escalation needs; identify affected operational procedures; anticipate likely safety evidence and assurance requirements early.
enablers.expected_outcome: Safety implications are understood before significant development decisions are made, allowing assurance, human oversight and evidence requirements to be incorporated progressively rather than discovered late in the project.
enablers.stakeholders: Legal / safety / compliance; Systems engineering; Maintenance / operations; Asset management; Data science / AI teams; IT / data platform

questions.text: Does the company consistently require owned business problems, stakeholder-specific benefits and funded lifecycle business cases?
questions.criteria:
1114: business-approved problem definition and ownership
1133: stakeholder-specific benefits and success measures
1143: lifecycle investment logic and shared-foundation funding
questions.topic: Business problem and investment
questions.why_this_matters:
1114: A clear problem and empowered owner prevent investment in solutions that do not address a measurable operational need.
1133: Different groups may experience different benefits and burdens; a single generic value claim can hide objections.
1143: A promising pilot can become unsustainable when support, integration and shared-platform costs are omitted.
questions.what_to_consider:
Assess consistency across the named business units and initiatives. A single successful pilot does not establish company-wide capability.
1114: Check the affected process, baseline, decision authority, success measures and evidence that the business accepts the problem.
1133: Include operators, maintenance, IT, management and other affected groups. Check whose outcome is measured and who validated it.
1143: Review build and operating costs, benefits, uncertainty, funding approval and allocation of shared foundations.
questions.evidence_examples:
1114: Approved problem statement, baseline, process boundaries and accountable owner
1133: Stakeholder value propositions, benefit measures and recorded stakeholder feedback
1143: Business case, cost sensitivities, funding approvals and shared-cost allocation
questions.when_to_use_na: Use only if every mapped criterion is outside the documented assessment scope. Record why and who accepted the scope decision. A future-stage requirement or absent practice is not automatically N/A. Mixed applicability requires Expert assessment.
questions.when_to_use_dont_know: Use when the requirement may apply but you cannot establish the level from available evidence. Record the information needed and the person who can supply it. Excluded from maturity scoring and retained as an unresolved information gap.
questions.rubric_0:
At least one required element has no established practice: business-approved problem definition and ownership; stakeholder-specific benefits and success measures; lifecycle investment logic and shared-foundation funding.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1114: The team starts building a model without identifying the operational problem.
1133: Benefits are described only as using AI.
1143: Only a software purchase price is known.
questions.rubric_1:
A problem and benefits are discussed, but ownership and funding remain informal.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1114: A manager mentions inspection delays but no one accepts ownership.
1133: The team claims time savings without identifying who saves time.
1143: A spreadsheet estimates pilot costs but omits ongoing support.
questions.rubric_2:
Problem ownership, stakeholder benefits and lifecycle costs are documented, but at least one lacks validation or approval. Evidence may be limited to individual units or pilots.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1114: A problem statement exists but the delay baseline is unverified.
1133: Maintenance validates a benefit measure but dispatchers have not been consulted.
1143: Lifecycle costs are estimated but platform funding is unresolved.
questions.rubric_3:
An authorised owner approves the problem; all affected groups validate benefits; lifecycle risks, funding and shared costs are agreed. Required across all assessed units and relevant initiatives.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1114: The process owner approves the baseline and the intended improvement.
1133: Each affected group agrees its benefit measures and communication approach.
1143: Approvers fund the full lifecycle case and agree shared-cost allocation.
questions.rubric_4:
The owner reviews measured benefits, stakeholder feedback and actual lifecycle costs and uses them to revise priorities and funding. All level-3 conditions continue to be met. Demonstrated across repeated organisational review cycles.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1114: The owner compares results with the baseline and changes priorities when benefits fall short.
1133: Benefit reviews reveal extra operator workload and the rollout is adjusted.
1143: Actual support costs trigger a documented funding and scope adjustment.

questions.text: Are AI priorities aligned to a shared vision, coordinated across units and supported by timely governance and sustained sponsorship?
questions.criteria:
1211: shared AI vision and strategic alignment
1223: cross-unit prioritisation and coordination
1233: timely governance decisions and escalation
1243: sustained sponsorship and resource commitment
questions.topic: Strategy and decisions
questions.why_this_matters:
1211: A shared purpose gives teams a consistent basis for selecting and stopping AI initiatives.
1223: Uncoordinated initiatives compete for scarce people, data and platforms and can block one another.
1233: Unclear decisions and slow approvals can strand otherwise viable solutions between stages.
1243: Sustained sponsorship helps resolve organisational obstacles and protect resources through adoption.
questions.what_to_consider:
Assess consistency across the named business units and initiatives. A single successful pilot does not establish company-wide capability.
1211: Ask sponsors and delivery teams to explain the same strategic contribution in their own words. Check alignment in actual decisions.
1223: Check overlapping initiatives, shared resources, sequencing and how cross-unit conflicts are resolved.
1233: Check named approvers, authority, expected turnaround, escalation and recorded scale, adapt or stop decisions.
1243: Look for actions beyond endorsement: attendance, resource commitments, escalation resolution and continuity.
questions.evidence_examples:
1211: AI vision, strategic objectives and documented project alignment
1223: Portfolio decisions, prioritisation criteria and cross-unit agreements
1233: Governance charter, decision log, review calendar and escalation records
1243: Sponsor reviews, resource commitments and resolved escalations
questions.when_to_use_na: Use only if every mapped criterion is outside the documented assessment scope. Record why and who accepted the scope decision. A future-stage requirement or absent practice is not automatically N/A. Mixed applicability requires Expert assessment.
questions.when_to_use_dont_know: Use when the requirement may apply but you cannot establish the level from available evidence. Record the information needed and the person who can supply it. Excluded from maturity scoring and retained as an unresolved information gap.
questions.rubric_0:
At least one required element has no established practice: shared AI vision and strategic alignment; cross-unit prioritisation and coordination; timely governance decisions and escalation; sustained sponsorship and resource commitment.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1211: Teams cannot explain why AI is a priority.
1223: Two teams commit the same specialist without coordination.
1233: No one knows who can approve deployment.
1243: No senior sponsor is identified.
questions.rubric_1:
Leaders express an ambition, but priorities, decisions and sponsorship depend on individuals.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1211: Sponsors describe innovation while users expect workload reduction.
1223: Managers negotiate access informally when delivery dates collide.
1233: The team seeks approval through personal contacts.
1243: A sponsor endorses the concept but does not attend reviews.
questions.rubric_2:
Vision, priorities, governance roles and sponsorship are documented, but cross-unit conflicts or decision/resource commitments remain open. Evidence may be limited to individual units or pilots.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1211: A vision is written but different teams interpret success differently.
1223: Dependencies are documented but competing resource requests remain open.
1233: A review process exists but missed deadlines have no escalation route.
1243: Resources are promised for the pilot but not for rollout.
questions.rubric_3:
Teams share the AI vision; cross-unit priorities are agreed; timely decisions and sustained sponsor resources support delivery. Required across all assessed units and relevant initiatives.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1211: Sponsors and teams use the agreed vision to choose initiatives.
1223: A portfolio decision resolves shared-resource conflicts and sequencing.
1233: Named approvers record decisions and use the agreed escalation route.
1243: The sponsor resolves a staffing escalation and maintains rollout funding.
questions.rubric_4:
Strategic outcomes, portfolio conflicts, decision delays and resource continuity are reviewed and lead to coordinated improvements. All level-3 conditions continue to be met. Demonstrated across repeated organisational review cycles.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1211: Outcome reviews lead to an explicit revision of strategic priorities.
1223: Measured dependency delays lead to a revised portfolio allocation.
1233: Decision-time reviews remove a recurring approval bottleneck.
1243: Reviews identify weakening support early and secure replacement commitments.

questions.text: Are post-prototype business ownership, human decision accountability and funded operating models consistently established?
questions.criteria:
1314: business ownership beyond prototype
1323: human accountability for AI-supported decisions
1334: funded post-go-live operating model
questions.topic: Ownership and operation
questions.why_this_matters:
1314: Without post-pilot ownership, adoption and benefits can become nobody's responsibility.
1323: AI outputs need accountable human decisions, especially when recommendations are uncertain or disputed.
1334: A service cannot remain dependable without funded people and agreed responsibilities after go-live.
questions.what_to_consider:
Assess consistency across the named business units and initiatives. A single successful pilot does not establish company-wide capability.
1314: Separate technical delivery responsibility from business authority over adoption, process change and realised benefits.
1323: Map who acts, approves, owns outcomes, overrides and escalates for normal and failure scenarios.
1334: Check support hours, service levels, budget, staffing, ownership and escalation after the delivery team leaves.
questions.evidence_examples:
1314: Ownership acceptance, benefit accountability and post-pilot responsibilities
1323: Decision responsibility matrix, human oversight procedures and scenario exercises
1334: Service model, staffing, support budget and agreed service levels
questions.when_to_use_na: Use only if every mapped criterion is outside the documented assessment scope. Record why and who accepted the scope decision. A future-stage requirement or absent practice is not automatically N/A. Mixed applicability requires Expert assessment.
questions.when_to_use_dont_know: Use when the requirement may apply but you cannot establish the level from available evidence. Record the information needed and the person who can supply it. Excluded from maturity scoring and retained as an unresolved information gap.
questions.rubric_0:
At least one required element has no established practice: business ownership beyond prototype; human accountability for AI-supported decisions; funded post-go-live operating model.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1314: The pilot ends without a business owner.
1323: Operators receive recommendations with no decision responsibility defined.
1334: No support arrangement exists beyond the pilot.
questions.rubric_1:
Informal owners are suggested, but decision authority and service support are uncertain.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1314: A delivery lead is assumed to own adoption without business authority.
1323: Staff assume a supervisor will decide but have no agreed procedure.
1334: The data scientist informally handles all incidents.
questions.rubric_2:
Business owners, human decision roles and a run model are documented, but acceptance, testing or funding is incomplete. Evidence may be limited to individual units or pilots.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1314: A business owner is named but benefit accountability is unresolved.
1323: Roles are documented but an ambiguous recommendation has not been rehearsed.
1334: A service plan exists but night-shift support is unfunded.
questions.rubric_3:
Business ownership is accepted; human decision and escalation roles are tested; a staffed and funded service model is operational. Required across all assessed units and relevant initiatives.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1314: The owner accepts responsibility for adoption and realised benefits.
1323: An exercise confirms who overrides an output and who approves the alternative action.
1334: A funded support rota and accepted service levels cover the intended operation.
questions.rubric_4:
Benefits, oversight incidents and service performance are reviewed regularly and used to improve ownership and operating arrangements. All level-3 conditions continue to be met. Demonstrated across repeated organisational review cycles.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1314: An organisational change triggers a documented ownership transfer without interrupting benefit reviews.
1323: Incident reviews improve decision authority and escalation procedures.
1334: Service workload reviews lead to additional support capacity and improved response times.

questions.text: Do teams have the skills, user trust and capacity needed to adopt AI and absorb continuing change?
questions.criteria:
1413: role-specific AI and digital competence
1424: user involvement and evidence-based trust
1433: capacity to absorb rollout and continuing change
questions.topic: People and change
questions.why_this_matters:
1413: Skill gaps can undermine delivery, safe use and ongoing support even when the technology works.
1424: Trust and adoption depend on user experience and how concerns affect design and working practices.
1433: Operational teams need time and support to absorb rollout and repeated updates without overloading existing work.
questions.what_to_consider:
Assess consistency across the named business units and initiatives. A single successful pilot does not establish company-wide capability.
1413: Assess competence by role and demonstrated tasks, not training attendance alone. Include users and support staff.
1424: Include affected user groups, job-impact concerns, trial participation, response records and observed uptake.
1433: Check allocated learning time, concurrent changes, workload, change ownership and support for later releases.
questions.evidence_examples:
1413: Role-based skills assessment, training records and demonstrated competence
1424: User engagement, trial feedback, adoption evidence and concern-resolution records
1433: Change workload assessment, allocated capacity, learning plan and adoption reviews
questions.when_to_use_na: Use only if every mapped criterion is outside the documented assessment scope. Record why and who accepted the scope decision. A future-stage requirement or absent practice is not automatically N/A. Mixed applicability requires Expert assessment.
questions.when_to_use_dont_know: Use when the requirement may apply but you cannot establish the level from available evidence. Record the information needed and the person who can supply it. Excluded from maturity scoring and retained as an unresolved information gap.
questions.rubric_0:
At least one required element has no established practice: role-specific AI and digital competence; user involvement and evidence-based trust; capacity to absorb rollout and continuing change.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1413: No one has assessed the skills needed to use the solution.
1424: Users first hear about the solution at deployment.
1433: Rollout assumes staff will learn during normal duties.
questions.rubric_1:
Gaps and concerns are acknowledged, but training, involvement and change capacity are informal.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1413: Staff attend general AI sessions without role-specific objectives.
1424: Concerns are collected informally but do not affect design.
1433: Managers recognise extra work but allocate no time.
questions.rubric_2:
Training, user trials and a change plan have started, but competence, concern resolution or capacity is incomplete. Evidence may be limited to individual units or pilots.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1413: Role-based training starts but support competence remains untested.
1424: Pilot users give feedback but important concerns remain unanswered.
1433: A change plan exists but release training clashes with operational commitments.
questions.rubric_3:
Required roles demonstrate competence; user concerns are addressed through participation; rollout and update capacity is allocated. Required across all assessed units and relevant initiatives.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1413: Users and support teams demonstrate the tasks required before rollout.
1424: Affected groups trial the solution and see documented responses to concerns.
1433: Staff time and support are allocated for rollout and subsequent updates.
questions.rubric_4:
Competence, adoption, trust and change workload are measured and used to improve training, involvement and rollout support. All level-3 conditions continue to be met. Demonstrated across repeated organisational review cycles.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1413: Assessment results drive updated training and improved task performance.
1424: Usage and trust reviews lead to a verified improvement in the user workflow.
1433: Workload and adoption evidence leads to a slower rollout and revised support.

questions.text: Do realistic expectations of AI and documented comparisons of AI and non-AI approaches guide solution selection?
questions.criteria:
1511: realistic expectations of AI capabilities and limitations
3123: evidence-based solution and technology selection
questions.topic: Capability and solution choice
questions.why_this_matters:
1511: Realistic expectations reduce unsuitable use and prevent decisions based on exaggerated capabilities.
3123: Comparing alternatives prevents choosing AI or a platform that is unnecessarily complex or poorly suited to the task.
questions.what_to_consider:
Assess consistency across the named business units and initiatives. A single successful pilot does not establish company-wide capability.
1511: Check understanding of data needs, uncertainty, failure modes, accuracy limits and the intended operating boundary.
3123: Compare credible AI and non-AI options using operational requirements, scalability, costs and test results.
questions.evidence_examples:
1511: Capability briefings, assumptions register and agreed limitations
3123: Options assessment, benchmark results, selection criteria and decision rationale
questions.when_to_use_na: Use only if every mapped criterion is outside the documented assessment scope. Record why and who accepted the scope decision. A future-stage requirement or absent practice is not automatically N/A. Mixed applicability requires Expert assessment.
questions.when_to_use_dont_know: Use when the requirement may apply but you cannot establish the level from available evidence. Record the information needed and the person who can supply it. Excluded from maturity scoring and retained as an unresolved information gap.
questions.rubric_0:
At least one required element has no established practice: realistic expectations of AI capabilities and limitations; evidence-based solution and technology selection.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1511: Sponsors assume the model will always be correct.
3123: A model is selected before requirements are defined.
questions.rubric_1:
Selection follows demonstrations or vendor claims without understanding AI limitations.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1511: A successful demo is treated as proof of general reliability.
3123: A vendor demo determines the choice without comparison.
questions.rubric_2:
Capabilities, limitations and alternatives are documented, but stakeholder alignment or comparative testing is incomplete. Evidence may be limited to individual units or pilots.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1511: Limitations are documented but some users still expect autonomous decisions.
3123: An options matrix exists but key alternatives lack benchmarks.
questions.rubric_3:
Sponsors and users agree realistic AI limits; AI and non-AI alternatives are compared against operations, scale and lifecycle costs. Required across all assessed units and relevant initiatives.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
1511: Sponsors and users agree what the solution can and cannot support.
3123: Approvers select an option using documented comparative evidence.
questions.rubric_4:
Observed performance and costs update expectations and trigger evidence-based reassessment of the chosen approach. All level-3 conditions continue to be met. Demonstrated across repeated organisational review cycles.
Examples (illustrative, not actual findings):
